newsitem.title: GERMANY: Institutes say Germany to miss Maastricht targets.
newsitem.headline: Institutes say Germany to miss Maastricht targets.

text.p: Germany will fail to meet the strict debt and deficit criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1997 despite a stronger economy, the country's six leading economic research institutes said in a semi-annual report on Tuesday.
The institutes said Germany's 1997 public deficit would likely be 3.5 percent of economic output, above the 3.0 percent reference value specified in the Maastricht Treaty.
"The reference values for the deficit criterion and the debt criterion set in the Maastricht Treaty will not be reached in 1997, based on data available today," the report said.

Maastricht specifies that EMU participants' overall outstanding debt should be below 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), but the treaty gives considerable leeway on how the criteria will be applied.
1997 is the key year for deciding what countries will participate in EMU at the scheduled start in January 1999.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has projected Germany's deficit will be 2.5 percent of GDP in 1997, comfortably below the Maastricht target.
Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer have been among the most vocal advocates that the criteria be strictly interpreted to ensure the Euro will remain at least as stable as the German mark.

The institutes said German GDP was likely to grow 1.5 percent in 1996, rising to 2.5 percent growth in 1997. The 1996 projection was up from a forecast of 0.75 percent growth made by the same institutes six months ago.

The report said Germany's total public sector deficit will probably fall by 17 billion marks to 127 billion marks in 1997 as the rise in government spending is slowed and taxpayer withholdings are increased, but the deficit would still be 3.5 percent of GDP.
The institutes said the current level of interest rates is appropriate, but a slight tightening is possible if M3 money supply growth remains above target levels.
"At present neither interest rate cuts nor rises appear necessary," the institutes said. But the Bundesbank should not hesitate to raise interest rates slightly if M3 remains above target.
A slight tightening to bring M3 back into the target corridor would pose no danger of ending the economic upturn, the report said.
Unemployment is seen remaining high at 10.4 percent in 1997, up from 10.3 percent in 1996 and 9.4 percent in 1995.
Consumer price inflation is seen remaining subdued at 1.5 percent next year, unchanged from this year and down from 1.8 percent in 1995.
